items.text: AMEND AND RECOMMIT TO CHILDREN AND FAMILIES

items.actClause:
AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to the reporting of child
abuse
items.lawCode: Add Art 6 Title 6-B §§429-a - 429-d, Soc Serv L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S1257

SPONSOR: SERINO
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the social services law, in relation to the reporting of
child abuse

 
PURPOSE:

Requires certain persons and officials to report child abuse or
suspected child abuse to law enforcement authorities

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1: Adds a new title 6-B of the Social Services law to create
reporting requirements of suspected child abuse to law enforcement where
it does not involve a family member for the purposes of the social secu-
rity law. Adds a new provision for reporting by persons eighteen and
older who are employed or affiliated with an organization that provides
services or programming to children.  Provides for training requirements
for mandated reporting and directs the Commissioner of the Office of
Children and Family Services to prescribe a period of compliance to
receive updated training. Also provides for penalties for willful fail-
ure to report suspected abuse and immunity from liability for reporting
suspected abuse in good faith.

Section 2: Establishes the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

New York currently has a system in place mandating specified individuals
to report suspected child abuse or maltreatment. This system, however,
is constrained by the Family Court Act which defines an abused child as
"a child less than eighteen years of age whose parent or other person
legally responsible for his care" commits certain delineated acts. As a
result of this language, mandated reporters are only required to report
suspected instances of child abuse that occur in a domestic setting.
However, as countless recent cases indicate, all too often abuse happens
at the hands of those outside of the family, by those persons known to
the child who have often have a position of trust or authority in their
lives.

For example, in Dutchess County, a prominent County Legislator and Boy
Scout Troop Leader was convicted of sexually abusing two boy scouts in
his troop. Although the boys reported the abuse to a person within the
Boy Scout organization, the allegations were never reported to the
parents or even law enforcement. This case is not unusual as the majori-
ty of child sexual abuse happens at the hands of someone that the child
knows and trusts. In fact, according to the National Sex Offender Public
Registry, 60% of those who sexually abuse children turn out to be indi-
viduals known to the child, but are not family members.

This bill will strengthen the law by amending the mandatory reporting
section of the Social Services Law to construct a system for these indi-
viduals, as well as individuals eighteen and older who are employed or
affiliated - paid or unpaid - with an organization that provides
services and programming to children, to report suspected cases of child
abuse outside of the domestic setting. These reports will be required to
go directly to law enforcement and will close a significant loophole in
the current system in New York and ensure that we have a robust process
of reporting and investigation.

This mandatory reporting requirement will help bring victims out of the
shadows and assist in identifying more unreported/under-reported cases
of abuse in our communities and establish another significant investi-
gative tool for law enforcement.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

2018: S.2158C Passed Senate
2017: S.2158A Reported to Finance
2016: S.8151 Referred to Rules

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
On the sixtieth day after it shall have become a law.
